Perseus. The son of Zeus and the mortal princess Danae, raised in exile and destined for greatness. He is most renowned for slaying Medusa, the terrifying Gorgon whose gaze turned men to stone, a triumph of impossible odds that ranks him among the greatest heroes of Greek mythology.

His mother Danae was locked away in a bronze tower by her fearful father, a king who sought to prevent the fulfillment of a prophecy. Yet Zeus found a way to reach her, and Perseus was born of their union. The boy and his mother were cast away, but they survived. As he grew, Perseus became aware of the trials that awaited him.

To hunt Medusa seemed like a suicide mission. The Gorgon was one of three monstrous sisters, each with serpents for hair and the power to turn anyone who looked upon her into stone. But Odysseus was not alone. The goddess Athena took an interest in the young hero and provided her guidance. Hermes, the messenger god, appeared and gave him extraordinary gifts—a magical sickle of adamantine and winged sandals that would let him fly.

With these divine aids, Perseus journeyed to the edge of the world where Medusa dwelt. He approached carefully, using his polished shield as a mirror so he could see Medusa without meeting her deadly gaze directly. As she slept, he struck with his magical sickle and severed her head from her body. The weapon retained its petrifying power even in death—a tool of extraordinary potency.

But Perseus's trials were not yet over. With the severed head of Medusa and his divine gifts, he made his way back across lands and seas. He came upon a princess named Andromeda who was chained to a rock as a sacrifice to a sea monster sent by Poseidon. Using Medusa's head as a weapon, he turned the monster to stone and rescued the princess. He fell in love with her and married her, taking her as his bride.

Yet even as he achieved his victories, fate was not finished with him. He had been destined, long before his birth, to cause the death of his grandfather—the same king who had locked his mother away. Despite all his efforts and the efforts of those who loved him to prevent this prophecy, it came to pass. His greatest triumphs could not forestall the will of fate itself.
